editorContent.value: Trials are voluntary at every step — here’s how a typical journey unfolds, from first conversation through follow-up care.

editorContent.label: Text
editorContent.value: Talk with your oncologist about whether a trial fits your diagnosis, treatment history, and goals.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Eligibility review based on labs, imaging, and your molecular profile to match you with the right trial.

editorContent.label: Text
editorContent.value: Informed consent, baseline tests, and a clear study schedule before any treatment begins.

editorContent.label: Text
editorContent.value: Receive the trial therapy with close monitoring and continued support from your full care team.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: If you don’t see your question here, our research team is happy to answer it directly — reach out to either program above.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: A clinical trial is a carefully designed research study that tests new treatments in patients. All trials are reviewed and approved by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) to ensure patient safety, and participation is always voluntary.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Most cancer clinical trials do not use placebos alone. When a control arm is included, participants always receive at least the current standard of care in addition to any investigational agent.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Investigational drugs and study-related tests are typically provided at no cost. Standard-of-care costs (like routine blood work) are generally billed to your insurance as they normally would be.

editorContent.label: Text
editorContent.value: How do I find out if I’m eligible?

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Ask your oncologist about trial options at your next visit, or contact our research team directly. We’ll review your diagnosis, treatment history, and molecular profile to identify suitable trials.

editorContent.label: Text
editorContent.value: Can I leave a trial if I change my mind?

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Yes. Participation is entirely voluntary. You may withdraw from a clinical trial at any time, for any reason, without affecting your ongoing care at Utah Cancer Specialists.

editorContent.value: Dale measures his life in rivers. Forty years of early mornings, waders, and the particular quiet of moving water. So when persistent night sweats and a swollen lymph node turned out to be non-Hodgkin lymphoma, his first question wasn’t about survival rates. It was: “Will I fish again?”

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: “My oncologist didn’t laugh,” Dale says. “He said, ‘That’s the goal. Let’s build the treatment around getting you back on the water.’ That was the moment I trusted him.”

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Treatment was hard — six cycles of chemotherapy through a Utah winter. The care team at the Ogden clinic scheduled his infusions so his strongest days landed on weekends, when his son could drive him to the Weber River just to watch it run. By spring, watching had turned back into wading.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Three years cancer-free, Dale ties his own flies again and has taught both grandsons to cast. “People ask me what beating cancer feels like,” he says. “It feels like cold water around your knees at sunrise. It feels like being exactly where you belong.”

editorContent.value: In June 2019, a seizure brought Dukhi Hong to the emergency room. Doctors diagnosed small cell lung cancer that had spread to her brain, and estimated that she had six to nine months to live.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Six years later, at age 84, she reached her 100th immunotherapy treatment at Utah Cancer Specialists. Visits every three to four weeks had become occasions for her family to gather and celebrate time together.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Her oncologist, Dr. Stephan Kendall, described the milestone as extraordinary. The March 2025 account reported no signs of cancer in her lungs and minimal activity in her brain. Her response was unusual, not a prediction of how others would respond.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Dukhi moved from South Korea to Utah in 1965 and later raised four children as a single mother. Her daughter, Mitzi Maughan, described her as a source of strength and inspiration.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: For the family, the hundredth treatment meant more than a number: it marked years of shared memories, and the chance for more time with someone they loved.

editorContent.value: At 27, Jasmine was training for her first marathon when a routine physical found something that wasn’t routine at all: Hodgkin lymphoma. “I remember thinking — I’m the healthiest person I know,” she says. “I run fifty miles a week. How is this happening?”

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Her team at Utah Cancer Specialists never asked her to stop being a runner. They asked her what pace she wanted to set. Her treatment plan was built around her training calendar — infusions on Mondays so she could jog easy by Friday, bloodwork timed around her long runs, honest conversations about what her body could and couldn’t do each week.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: “There were weeks I could barely walk to the mailbox,” she admits. “But my nurse would say, ‘That’s today. It’s not every day.’ They treated my goals like they were part of the medicine. Because they were.”

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Eighteen months after her final treatment, Jasmine crossed the finish line of the Utah Valley Marathon. Her care team was at mile 26 with a sign. “Cancer is a chapter,” she says, lacing up at dawn like always. “It was never the whole story.”

editorContent.value: When Maria found the lump, she did what so many of us do: she waited. Two weeks of telling herself it was nothing, two weeks of not sleeping. When the diagnosis came back — invasive ductal carcinoma, stage II — the world she knew narrowed to a single word she could not stop hearing.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Her first appointment at Utah Cancer Specialists changed the shape of that word. “They drew it for me,” she remembers. “The doctor took out a piece of paper and drew what was happening in my body, and then drew what we were going to do about it. Nobody had done that. Suddenly there was a plan, and I was part of it.”

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Over fourteen months of treatment — surgery, chemotherapy, radiation — Maria’s care team became a second family. Her patient advocate handled the insurance calls she dreaded. A nurse learned the names of her grandchildren. On her hardest day, someone simply sat with her and held her hand.

editorContent.label: Paragraph
editorContent.value: Today Maria is in remission and back in her garden, where the roses she planted the spring of her diagnosis have bloomed three times over. “Cancer took a year from me,” she says. “But this team gave me all the years after it back.”
